title: I made a free, open-source tool that turns a character description into a 32×32 sprite sheet with walk cycles and Godot/Unity imports
author: JuanixVentures
selftext:
TL;DR: runs locally on an NVIDIA GPU. Examples with the exact prompts: https://mcpbytes.github.io/mcpbytes-pixel-sprite/

    uvx --torch-backend=auto mcpbytes-pixel-sprite generate "a forest ranger with a green hood"

The first run downloads about 16 GB of model files. Results go to ./pixel-sprites/.

I'm the developer. The point is characters you can drop straight into an engine, not just a nice picture. You describe a character and get a 128×128 sheet of sixteen 32×32 cells: three walk poses facing down, left, right and up, plus four still poses (arms raised, jump left, jump right, lying down).

How it works:

1. FLUX.2 [klein] base 4B with svntax-dev's pixel spritesheet LoRA renders a 512×512 sheet. Your description sits inside a fixed layout prompt: four rows of four cells on a plain magenta background.
2. After that it's ordinary CPU image processing, no second model. It removes the magenta and the pink fringe it leaves on edges, downscales to 128×128, maps the sheet to one shared palette (16, 32 or 64 colours, or your own hex list) and cuts the 16 frames.
3. It writes looping walk GIFs, JSON with frame rectangles and pivots, a Godot 4 scene, a Unity 6 importer that builds the clips and a prefab, and the raw render so you can see what the model drew before cleanup.

The same seed and inputs on the same GPU and memory mode give you the same files byte for byte. It also runs as an MCP server, so Claude, Cursor and other MCP clients can make sprites themselves.

What it won't do: the walk is three drawn poses played 1-2-3-2, not a hand-animated cycle. Four directions only, small characters only, no custom actions. Details can drift between rows, so every result is flagged for review instead of approved.

Hardware: NVIDIA with a CUDA 12.8 driver on Windows or Linux. It picks a memory mode from your card, and the slowest mode needs about 1 GB of VRAM. The code is AGPL-3.0, the importer script and guide it copies into each export are MIT-0, and what you generate is yours.

Repo: https://github.com/MCPBytes/mcpbytes-pixel-sprite

If you try it, tell me where it breaks. Weird prompts welcome.
